extracted.intended_audience: early-career mathematicians, graduate students and researchers making career/field-choice decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing research areas and assessing what counts as 'good' mathematics, aimed at informing career decisions for mathematicians. Emphasizes long-term strategy (foundations, intrinsic interest) over chasing glamour or fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base career decisions on glamour or fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Going into a field 'simply because it is glamorous is not a good idea.' There is little glamour to chase, and chasing it is the wrong primary objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat glamour/fame as an unreliable and poor primary motive for choosing a research area; avoid letting perceived celebrity drive your field selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation before fame
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile work attracts intense competition; success requires 'solid backgrounds' with experience in less glamorous aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize building a strong technical foundation and experience in foundational or less-publicized subareas before attempting high-visibility problems; recognize that glamour sites the most competition and demands deeper preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue incremental progress via simpler model problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Famous unsolved problems rarely yield to fresh approaches; invest in 'simpler model problems, acquiring techniques, intuition, partial results, context, and literature' first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on toy or model problems to develop methods and intuition. Value partial results and contextual knowledge as stepping stones toward harder problems instead of expecting immediate breakthroughs on famous questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value intrinsic interest over recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to 'produce good mathematics and contribute to your field, and the prizes and recognition will take care of themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let genuine curiosity and the desire to contribute guide your research choices rather than short-term metrics of recognition; long-run excellence commonly precedes awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer specific institutional strengths to general prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose institutions based on their concrete strengths in areas relevant to you rather than overall prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutions for alignment with your research interests (mentors, groups, technical resources) rather than chasing high-status names that may not support your actual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate authentic interest in problems and areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Value 'authentic interest' in problems/areas as a criterion for selecting research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics you find genuinely engaging; sustained motivation improves the likelihood of producing meaningful, lasting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the reasons behind renown
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand 'why problems or mathematicians are renowned (not just their fame)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the substantive reasons a problem or researcher is celebrated (techniques, connections, impact) rather than imitating surface-level prestige; this helps identify tractable entry points and meaningful contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on long-term contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Value 'long-term contribution' as the measure of good mathematical work rather than immediate notoriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess research by its lasting value and the ways it enables further work, not by short-term visibility or hype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize solid, foundational work that enables breakthroughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce 'solid, foundational work' that provides groundwork for future breakthroughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize rigorous, foundational results and framework-building that other researchers can build on; such enabling work often precedes and underpins major advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate 'good' mathematics by intrinsic motivation and contribution, not celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' piece of math is intrinsically motivated, built on careful groundwork, and measured by contribution — not celebrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging research quality (your own or others'), emphasize intrinsic intellectual merit, rigor, context, and contribution to the field rather than external markers like fame or media attention.
